You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

name: continual-arc
description: Solve Continual-ARC grid instances; follow the per-turn action protocol, infer transformations from demonstrations, and use feedback to choose the next action.
---

# Continual ARC

1. Treat the puzzle protocol as the entire turn contract: do not add narration or invoke unrelated tools. On every turn, emit exactly one valid protocol-action JSON object and nothing else; every feedback turn needs an action too. Do not defer an action while reasoning or use tools that the puzzle contract does not require. Check action fields, grid dimensions, and cell values before submitting.
2. Track demo and wrong-attempt budgets. For every demo, align input and output cellwise and record the exact changed coordinates and color substitutions before inferring a rule. Identify separators/regions only when present; compare candidate regions, overlap/masking, orientation, and mappings across pairs. Do not interpret an unchanged demo as evidence for a transformation, or assume a panel is recolored wholesale merely because it resembles the test. Keep hypotheses distinct until examples discriminate them.
3. Request a demo only when a specific unresolved distinction could change the answer and another pair can resolve it; count it against the same cost as a wrong submission. Before requesting, state internally what competing rules it will distinguish. Stop requesting once evidence resolves the mapping; don't use demos as generic exploration. Infer color substitutions only for demonstrated mappings, and request only if a new pair can reveal an unknown test-color mapping.
4. Before submitting, apply the validated rule cellwise and preserve everything outside predicted changes. Respect orientation: Hx1 is a vertical line, not a 1xH row; verify output height and width independently and map cells along the actual axis. If using code, verify output dimensions and all cells. After incorrect feedback, eliminate the rejected hypothesis and materially revise using every demo; never repeat the same grid, a masked variant, or another guess that changes only an unsupported detail. A remembered rule for the same task family remains only a hypothesis until current shape, region, and index mapping are confirmed. Treat a wrong submission as evidence against the entire applied rule, not as a prompt to improvise unsupported edits: trace the demos to determine which inference failed before attempting again.
5. Stop only when the instance reports success/over or the attempt cap is reached; use `finish` only when allowed by the protocol.

It seems essential to understand how markers relate to colors in the corresponding cells. Finally, I’ll aim to output one JSON exactly.

 "path": "memory/continual-arc-task-eb4da30a.md",
 "content": "# Continual-ARC task-eb4da30a: hollow rectangular frame + two outside markers

Solved test instance (10x10), verified correct after one wrong submission and one demo.

## Demonstration
A 10x10 grid had hollow rectangular frame of color 5: outer border rows 2 and 7, columns 2 and 7 (0-based); its interior rows 3-6, cols 3-6 was blank. Outside the frame, markers were color 4 at (1,1) and color 8 at (1,8). Output left frame and markers unchanged, filled the interior in four 2x2 quadrants: rows 3-4 cols 3-4 = 4; rows 3-4 cols 5-6 = 8; rows 5-6 cols 3-4 = 8; rows 5-6 cols 5-6 = 4. Thus marker colors from upper-left and upper-right outside the frame map to a 2x2 checkerboard of solid quadrants: A B / B A.

## Solved test
Same frame geometry, markers at (8,1)=9 and (8,8)=1, i.e. below the frame. Correct interior was: rows 3-4 cols 3-4 = 1; rows 3-4 cols 5-6 = 9; rows 5-6 cols 3-4 = 9; rows 5-6 cols 5-6 = 1. This is the same A B / B A quadrant pattern, where A is the right-hand marker color and B the left-hand marker color when the two markers are beneath the frame. All other cells preserved.

## Caution / failed hypothesis
I initially assigned bottom markers in left-to-right order as top-row quadrants (9 left, 1 right), producing [9,1;1,9], which was incorrect. Correct bottom-marker mapping is reversed horizontally on the top interior row: top-left gets the right marker, top-right gets the left marker; bottom row of quadrants swaps those. For the demo's markers above the frame, ordinary left/right assignment yielded [4,8;8,4]. Preserve frame, markers, and all background.
"
